stem: A 3-year-old boy has had itchy, dry, red patches in the creases of his elbows and behind his knees for months. His father has asthma and hay fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Itchy dry eczematous patches in the flexures of a young child with a family history of atopy is atopic eczema. Psoriasis favours extensor surfaces with silvery scale, and seborrhoeic dermatitis affects the scalp, face and nappy area in infants.

stem: A 5-year-old girl with known atopic eczema suddenly develops painful, punched-out erosions and clustered vesicles over her eczematous face, with fever and malaise. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Rapidly spreading painful clustered vesicles and punched-out erosions over eczema with fever is eczema herpeticum, a dermatological emergency treated with aciclovir (IV if severe). Increasing topical steroids would worsen the viral infection.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who works as a cleaner has itchy, red, fissured skin on the backs of her hands, which improves on holidays. What is the most important measure to prevent recurrence?
explanation: Hand eczema that improves away from work suggests irritant contact dermatitis from detergents and water; avoidance, protective gloves and regular emollients are the key measures. Antihistamines do little for eczema itch, and antifungals treat tinea, not dermatitis.

stem: A 30-year-old man has well-demarcated red plaques with thick silvery scale on his elbows, knees and scalp. His nails show pitting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Well-demarcated red plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces and scalp, with nail pitting, are typical of chronic plaque psoriasis. Tinea has an active scaly edge with central clearing, and lichen planus produces purple polygonal papules.

stem: A 17-year-old boy develops many small, drop-like scaly red papules over his trunk 2 weeks after a sore throat. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Guttate psoriasis presents with numerous small teardrop scaly papules on the trunk, typically 2-3 weeks after a streptococcal throat infection in young people. Pityriasis rosea starts with a single herald patch followed by oval patches along skin lines.

stem: A 45-year-old man with psoriasis was started on a drug for another condition, and his psoriasis has become much worse. Which drug is most likely responsible?
explanation: Lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials such as chloroquine, and withdrawal of systemic steroids are well known to worsen psoriasis. Paracetamol, omeprazole and amlodipine are not typical triggers.

stem: Several children in a madrassa hostel in Peshawar have intense itching that is worse at night. Examination shows papules and burrows in the finger webs, wrists and around the waist. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Oral cetirizine at bedtime for all
Topical hydrocortisone 1% to all itchy areas
explanation: Nocturnal itch, burrows in the finger webs and wrists, and spread among close contacts indicate scabies; permethrin 5% applied from the neck down, repeated after a week, is used to treat all contacts at the same time, with washing of bedding. Antihistamines and steroids only relieve itch and do not kill the mite.

stem: A frail 80-year-old woman in a care home has thick, crusted, scaly plaques on her hands and feet with little itching. Several staff members now have an itchy rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Crusted scabies occurs in elderly or immunocompromised people, with hyperkeratotic crusts teeming with mites and often little itch; it is highly contagious, explaining the staff cases. It requires oral ivermectin with topical treatment and infection-control measures.

stem: A 25-year-old man was treated correctly for scabies with permethrin 2 weeks ago. He still has some itching but no new burrows. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Itching may persist for weeks after cure
Repeat permethrin every week for 2 months
Treatment has failed, so start oral ivermectin
Start a potent topical steroid on the whole body
explanation: Post-scabetic itch can persist for 2-6 weeks after successful treatment, as a hypersensitivity reaction to dead mites; emollients and an antihistamine help. New burrows or lesions would suggest treatment failure or reinfection.

stem: A 22-year-old man in Karachi has an itchy, ring-shaped rash on his groin and inner thighs, spreading outwards with a raised scaly edge and central clearing. The scrotum is spared. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: An itchy, annular lesion with an active scaly edge and central clearing in the groin that spares the scrotum is tinea cruris, a dermatophyte infection. Candidal intertrigo often involves the scrotum and has satellite pustules.

stem: A 19-year-old man has many pale and light brown, finely scaly patches on his upper back and chest that became more obvious after sunbathing. Skin scrapings show 'spaghetti and meatballs' hyphae and spores. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Pityriasis versicolor, caused by Malassezia yeast, gives hypo- or hyperpigmented scaly patches on the trunk with a 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance on microscopy, and is treated with topical azoles or selenium sulfide. Griseofulvin is ineffective against Malassezia.

stem: An 8-year-old boy has a scaly, itchy patch of hair loss on his scalp with broken hairs, and a tender boggy swelling on the scalp has now developed. Fungal culture grows Trichophyton. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Incision and drainage of the swelling
explanation: Tinea capitis, including a kerion (inflammatory boggy swelling), needs oral antifungal therapy because topical agents do not penetrate the hair follicle. A kerion is not a bacterial abscess and should not be incised.

stem: A 26-year-old man returned to Lahore after working in a village in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. He has a painless nodule on his cheek that slowly enlarged over 2 months and has ulcerated, with a raised edge and a crust. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A slowly enlarging, painless nodule on exposed skin that ulcerates with a raised edge, in someone from an endemic area, is typical of cutaneous leishmaniasis ('oriental sore'), spread by sandflies. Basal cell carcinoma grows over years and is rare at 26.

stem: A 30-year-old man has a suspected cutaneous leishmaniasis ulcer on his forearm. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Slit-skin smear from the ulcer edge
Swab of the ulcer base for Gram stain
explanation: Cutaneous leishmaniasis is confirmed by finding Leishman-Donovan bodies (amastigotes) in a slit-skin smear, scraping or biopsy from the active edge of the lesion, with PCR where available. Serology is usually negative in localised cutaneous disease.

stem: A 9-year-old child has a single small cutaneous leishmaniasis lesion on the arm, not near a joint or the face. Which treatment is commonly used in Pakistan?
explanation: Small, uncomplicated cutaneous leishmaniasis lesions are commonly treated with intralesional pentavalent antimonials such as sodium stibogluconate or meglumine antimoniate, or with cryotherapy. Topical steroids worsen the infection and antibiotics treat only secondary bacterial infection.

stem: A 16-year-old girl has open and closed comedones on her forehead and a few small inflamed papules. There are no nodules or scars. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Oral doxycycline alone for 6 months or more
explanation: Mild acne with comedones and few papules is treated with topical therapy, such as a topical retinoid combined with benzoyl peroxide. Oral isotretinoin is reserved for severe nodulocystic or scarring acne, and oral antibiotics should not be used alone.

stem: A 22-year-old woman with severe nodulocystic acne and scarring has failed oral antibiotics and is to start oral isotretinoin. Which measure is mandatory before and during treatment?
options: Weekly full blood count with blood film
explanation: Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic, so women must use effective contraception with regular pregnancy tests before, during and for a period after treatment; liver function and lipids are also monitored. Patients should avoid excessive sun because of skin sensitivity.

stem: A 23-year-old woman has acne, irregular periods and excess facial hair. She is overweight. Which underlying condition should be considered?
explanation: Acne with hirsutism and irregular periods in an overweight woman suggests hyperandrogenism from polycystic ovary syndrome; a combined oral contraceptive can help both acne and cycles. Hypothyroidism and Addison disease do not cause androgen excess.

stem: A 28-year-old man started carbamazepine 3 weeks ago. He now has fever, painful mouth ulcers, red eyes and dusky target-like lesions with blistering and skin detachment over 8% of his body surface. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Continue the drug and add an antihistamine
explanation: Fever, mucosal involvement and blistering with skin detachment under 10% of body surface after a new drug is Stevens-Johnson syndrome; the culprit drug must be stopped immediately and the patient managed like a burn, with eye care. Carbamazepine is a common cause, especially in carriers of HLA-B*15:02.

stem: A 40-year-old man has a single round, dusky red-violet patch on his lip that blisters, and it recurs at exactly the same site each time he takes co-trimoxazole, leaving brown pigmentation. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: A fixed drug eruption recurs at the same site each time the drug is taken, often on the lips, genitals or hands, and heals with hyperpigmentation; sulfonamides, NSAIDs and tetracyclines are common causes. Herpes labialis recurs but with grouped vesicles and no drug link.

stem: A 4-year-old child has mild atopic eczema with dry skin and occasional itchy patches. What is the mainstay of long-term management?
options: Potent topical steroid applied daily for months
explanation: Liberal, regular emollients and avoiding soap are the foundation of eczema care, with short courses of mild topical steroids for flares. Long-term potent steroids cause skin atrophy, and oral steroids are not used for mild eczema.

stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic plaque psoriasis covering 25% of his body has not improved with topical treatment and phototherapy. Which drug is a standard first-line systemic option?
explanation: Methotrexate is a first-line systemic agent for extensive psoriasis not controlled by topical therapy and phototherapy, alongside ciclosporin and acitretin. Systemic corticosteroids are avoided because withdrawal can trigger severe pustular or erythrodermic flares.

stem: An 18-month-old child has scabies with lesions on the palms, soles and scalp. How does the presentation in infants differ from adults?
options: Lesions may involve the face, scalp, palms and soles
Burrows are never seen in infants
Lesions are confined to the genitals and buttocks in infants
explanation: In infants and young children, scabies can involve the face, scalp, palms and soles, which are usually spared in adults, and may present with vesicles or pustules. Permethrin is applied to the whole body including the scalp and face in this age group.

stem: A 45-year-old diabetic man has a thickened, yellow, crumbling big toenail. Fungal culture grows Trichophyton rubrum. He wants treatment. Which is the most effective option?
explanation: Dermatophyte onychomycosis of the toenail responds best to oral terbinafine for about 12 weeks, after checking liver function. Topical creams do not penetrate the nail plate, and short courses are not sufficient.

stem: A 30-year-old man treated in childhood for visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) now has multiple hypopigmented macules and nodules on his face. Slit-skin smears show Leishman-Donovan bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis develops months or years after treated visceral leishmaniasis, with hypopigmented macules, papules and nodules, often on the face; the lesions contain parasites. Leprosy can look similar, but smears would show acid-fast bacilli rather than amastigotes.

stem: A 17-year-old boy has moderate inflammatory acne with many papules and pustules on his face and back, not improving after 3 months of topical treatment. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Oral isotretinoin at full dose straight away
Oral doxycycline alone for at least a year
explanation: Moderate inflammatory acne not responding to topical therapy is treated with an oral tetracycline such as doxycycline for up to about 3 months, combined with a topical retinoid or benzoyl peroxide to reduce resistance. Isotretinoin is reserved for severe or scarring acne or failure of these measures.
